title: Causal ML for Treatment Outcomes: Smoking, BMI, and Diabetes
text:
Feuerriegel et al. (2024) argue that standard ML pipelines fail when estimating treatment effects because they ignore the causal structure linking treatment, mediators, and outcomes. Their canonical example:

“Consider a patient with a high body mass index whose doctor recommends quitting smoking, and for whom the diabetes risk should be predicted. Literature from traditional ML would suggest using both the body mass index and smoking behavior to predict the diabetes risk under a smoking versus no-smoking scenario; however, this approach would ignore that stopping smoking would also change a patient’s body mass index.”

This document implements a principled causal analysis of exactly that example using three approaches:








Approach
Description
Validity




(A) Naïve ML
Logistic regression on post-treatment BMI
❌ Biased (conditions on mediator)


(B) Causal mediation
Decomposes total effect into direct + BMI-mediated (Imai, Keele, and Tingley 2010)
✅ Correct decomposition


(C) G-formula / SCM
Intervenes do(quit=1), propagates through BMI
✅ Correct counterfactual ATE





The synthetic cohort is calibrated to three published sources:

Hu et al. (2018) (NHS / NHS-II / HPFS cohorts, NEJM): post-cessation weight gain explained ~68% of the transient type 2 diabetes (T2D) spike; HR ≈ 1.91 for quitters with ≥10 kg gain.
Kangbuk Samsung Health Study (2024): mean BMI 25.68 ± 3.53 (T2D) vs 23.18 ± 3.28 (non-T2D); current smokers HR ≈ 1.29.
Bush et al. (2016): post-cessation BMI increase ≈ 0.9 kg/m² within 3 years; magnitude varies with baseline BMI.

text:
3 Causal DAG
The assumed structural equation model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{BMI}_0 &= 23.5 + 0.05(\text{Age}-50) + 1.20\,\text{Sex} + 0.50\,\text{FamHx}
               + 0.04\,\text{Alcohol} - 0.80\,\text{Activity} + \varepsilon_1,
               \quad \varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 3.0^2) \\[4pt]
\text{Quit}  &\sim \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(\sigma\!\left(
               -1.2 + 0.015(\text{Age}-50) - 0.20\,\text{Sex}
               + 0.02(\text{BMI}_0 - 23) + 0.30\,\text{Activity}\right)\right) \\[4pt]
\Delta\text{BMI} &= 0.90\,\text{Quit} + 0.05(\text{BMI}_0 - 23)\cdot\text{Quit}
                   + 0.30(1-\text{Activity})\cdot\text{Quit}
                   - 0.15\,\text{Activity} + \varepsilon_2,
                   \quad \varepsilon_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1.2^2) \\[4pt]
\text{logit}\,P(\text{T2D}=1) &= -5.50 + 0.035(\text{Age}-50) + 0.50\,\text{Sex}
               + 0.80\,\text{FamHx} + 0.20\,(\text{BMI}_0 + \Delta\text{BMI} - 23) \\
               &\quad + 0.025\,\text{Alcohol} - 0.40\,\text{Activity}
                 \underbrace{- 0.30\,\text{Quit}}_{\text{direct effect}} + \varepsilon_3,
                 \quad \varepsilon_3 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3^2)
\end{aligned}
\] The direct causal effect of quitting on T2D is encoded as \(-0.30\) on the log-odds scale. This is not directly comparable to the ATE and ADE reported by the g-formula and causal mediation analysis, which are both on the risk difference (probability) scale. At a baseline T2D prevalence of approximately 5%, a log-odds change of \(-0.30\) translates to a risk difference of roughly \(0.05 \times (1-0.05) \times 0.30 \approx 0.014\). However, the mediated pathway partially offsets this: quitting raises BMI by approximately \(+0.90\) kg/m² on average, and each unit of BMI increases log-odds of T2D by \(+0.20\), contributing an opposing mediated effect of approximately \(0.90 \times 0.20 = +0.18\) log-odds, or \(+0.008\) on the risk difference scale. The expected values on the probability scale are therefore:



Quantity
Expected (probability scale)




ADE — direct protective effect of quitting
≈ −0.010 to −0.015


ACME — harm mediated via BMI gain
≈ +0.005 to +0.010


ATE — net total effect (ADE + ACME)
≈ −0.004 to −0.008



These are exactly the values recovered by the g-formula and causal mediation analysis, confirming that both methods correctly identify the SEM parameters. The near-zero ATE reflects the short-term reality documented by Hu et al. (2018): the direct benefit of cessation is substantially offset by weight gain in the years immediately following quitting.
The key path ignored by naïve ML is Quit → ΔBMI → T2D.


Code
library(ggplot2)

# Node positions
dag_nodes <- data.frame(
  node = c("Quit\nSmoking", "ΔBMI", "Diabetes", "Baseline\nBMI",
           "Age/Sex/\nFam Hx", "Alcohol/\nActivity"),
  x    = c(3, 5, 7, 3, 1, 1),
  y    = c(3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 1)
)

dag_coords <- setNames(dag_nodes[, c("x","y")], c("x","y"))
rownames(dag_coords) <- dag_nodes$node

# Colour palette
pal <- c("mediated" = "#1D9E75",   # green
         "direct"   = "#3B8BD4",   # blue
         "conf"     = "#888780")   # grey

# Helper: nudge start/end away from node centres + optional perpendicular offset
# so parallel edges between the same pair of nodes do not overlap.
nudge <- 0.38
off   <- 0.13   # perpendicular separation

make_edge <- function(fx, fy, tx, ty, type, y_off = 0) {
  dx  <- tx - fx; dy <- ty - fy
  len <- sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)
  ux  <- dx / len; uy <- dy / len
  # perpendicular unit vector
  px  <- -uy; py <- ux
  data.frame(
    x    = fx + ux * nudge + px * y_off,
    y    = fy + uy * nudge + py * y_off,
    xend = tx - ux * nudge + px * y_off,
    yend = ty - uy * nudge + py * y_off,
    type = type,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

# Confounder edges (grey) — no parallel overlap with coloured edges
conf_pairs <- list(
  c("Baseline\nBMI",     "ΔBMI"),
  c("Baseline\nBMI",     "Diabetes"),
  c("Age/Sex/\nFam Hx",  "Quit\nSmoking"),
  c("Age/Sex/\nFam Hx",  "Diabetes"),
  c("Alcohol/\nActivity", "ΔBMI"),
  c("Alcohol/\nActivity", "Diabetes")
)
edges_conf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conf_pairs, function(p)
  make_edge(dag_coords[p[1],"x"], dag_coords[p[1],"y"],
            dag_coords[p[2],"x"], dag_coords[p[2],"y"], "conf", 0)
))

# Mediated path: Quit→ΔBMI and ΔBMI→Diabetes — nudged upward (positive offset)
edges_mediated <- rbind(
  make_edge(dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","x"], dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","y"],
            dag_coords["ΔBMI","x"],          dag_coords["ΔBMI","y"],
            "mediated", y_off =  off),
  make_edge(dag_coords["ΔBMI","x"],     dag_coords["ΔBMI","y"],
            dag_coords["Diabetes","x"], dag_coords["Diabetes","y"],
            "mediated", y_off =  off)
)

# Direct effect: Quit→Diabetes as a downward-bowing curve (blue)
# so it is visually separate from the straight green mediated chain
direct_df <- data.frame(
  x    = dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","x"] + nudge,
  y    = dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","y"],
  xend = dag_coords["Diabetes","x"] - nudge,
  yend = dag_coords["Diabetes","y"]
)

arr <- arrow(length = unit(0.28, "cm"), type = "open", ends = "last")

ggplot() +
  # 1. confounder edges (grey)
  geom_segment(
    data      = edges_conf,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["conf"],
    linewidth = 0.7,
    alpha     = 0.75,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # 2. direct effect (blue curved arc bowing downward)
  geom_curve(
    data      = direct_df,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["direct"],
    linewidth = 1.1,
    curvature = -0.30,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # 3. mediated path (green straight segments nudged upward)
  geom_segment(
    data      = edges_mediated,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["mediated"],
    linewidth = 1.4,
    arrow     = arr
  ) +
  # Node labels on top of everything
  geom_label(
    data          = dag_nodes,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = node),
    size          = 3.2,
    fill          = "white",
    colour        = "#1a1a1a",
    label.size    = 0.45,
    label.padding = unit(0.35, "lines")
  ) +
  # Annotation: mediator label above the green arrow
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 3.38,
           label  = "Mediator path\n(BMI gain)",
           size   = 2.9,
           colour = "#085041",
           fontface = "bold") +
  # Annotation: "ignored by naïve ML" below
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 2.58,
           label    = "Ignored by naïve ML",
           size     = 2.7,
           colour   = "#993C1D",
           fontface = "italic") +
  # Manual legend using dummy data
  geom_segment(
    data = data.frame(
      x    = c(0,0,0), y    = c(0,0,0),
      xend = c(0,0,0), yend = c(0,0,0),
      type = c("mediated","direct","conf")
    ),
    aes(x=x, y=y, xend=xend, yend=yend, colour=type),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = pal,
    labels = c("mediated" = "Mediated path (Quit → ΔBMI → T2D)",
               "direct"   = "Direct effect  (Quit → T2D)",
               "conf"     = "Confounder / covariate"),
    breaks = c("mediated", "direct", "conf")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Causal DAG: Smoking cessation → ΔBMI → Diabetes",
    subtitle = "Hu et al. (2018) NEJM; Kangbuk Samsung cohort (2024)",
    colour   = NULL, x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 8), ylim = c(0.2, 6)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text     = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm")
  )





Causal DAG. The mediated path (green) through ΔBMI is what naïve ML ignores when it conditions on post-treatment BMI.

4 Synthetic cohort


Code
set.seed(2024)
n <- 2000

# Baseline covariates
age      <- round(rnorm(n, 50, 10))
sex      <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45)          # 1 = male
fam_hx   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.20)         # family history of T2D
alcohol  <- pmax(0, rnorm(n, 8, 5))    # g/day
activity <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.35)         # physically active

# Baseline BMI — smokers slightly leaner (MR evidence, Atkins 2021)
bmi0 <- 23.5 +
  0.05 * (age - 50) + 1.20 * sex + 0.50 * fam_hx +
  0.04 * alcohol   - 0.80 * activity + rnorm(n, sd = 3.0)
bmi0 <- pmax(16, bmi0)

# Treatment: quit smoking
lp_quit <- -1.2 + 0.015*(age-50) - 0.20*sex + 0.02*(bmi0-23) + 0.30*activity
quit    <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_quit))

# Mediator: post-cessation BMI change
# Calibrated to Bush (2016): mean gain ≈ +0.9 kg/m² for quitters.
# Interaction coefficient 0.15 (increased from 0.05) to produce a
# detectable CATE gradient across BMI groups: a patient at BMI=30
# gains 0.15*(30-23)=1.05 kg/m² extra vs a patient at BMI=23.
delta_bmi <- 0.90 * quit +
             0.15 * (bmi0 - 23) * quit +   # stronger BMI×quit interaction
             0.30 * (1 - activity) * quit - # sedentary quitters gain more
             0.15 * activity + rnorm(n, sd = 1.2)

bmi_post <- bmi0 + delta_bmi

# Outcome: incident T2D (~5-year risk)
# Calibrated to HR ≈ 1.29 (smokers vs never, Kangbuk Samsung 2024)
# and BMI OR ≈ 1.10 per unit (Hu 2018)
lp_dm <- -5.50 +
  0.035 * (age - 50) + 0.50 * sex + 0.80 * fam_hx +
  0.20  * (bmi_post - 23) + 0.025 * alcohol - 0.40 * activity +
 -0.30  * quit + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)

diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_dm))

cohort <- data.frame(age, sex, fam_hx, alcohol, activity,
                     bmi0, quit, delta_bmi, bmi_post, lp_dm, diabetes)

5 Analysis A — Naïve ML (incorrect)
Logistic regression predicting T2D from (quit, bmi_post, covariates). This conditions on bmi_post, a post-treatment variable that lies on the causal path from quit to diabetes.

  diabetes ~ quit + bmi_post + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial

naive_coef <- coef(summary(naive_fit))

Why this is wrong — and what “underestimate” really means here



bmi_post is a mediator, not a baseline covariate. Including it in the outcome model as if it were fixed — independently of quit — blocks the quit → ΔBMI → T2D path.
To see the direction of the bias, recall that the outcome is diabetes risk (higher = worse) and the quit coefficient is negative (protective). By holding BMI fixed while varying quit, naïve ML asks: “What is the effect of quitting if BMI does not change?” This removes the harmful BMI-gain pathway, making quitting appear more protective than it really is. In other words:

Naïve ML overestimates the protective benefit of quitting (OR for quit is too far below 1.0).
As a consequence, it underestimates the true diabetes risk a quitter faces in the real world, where BMI does rise after cessation and partially offsets the direct benefit.
The causal analyses (B and C) recover a smaller protective effect — i.e. an ATE closer to zero — because they correctly propagate do(quit=1) → ΔBMI ↑ → T2D risk ↑, which partially cancels the direct protective path. This is precisely the short-term dynamic documented by Hu et al. (2018): the transient T2D spike after cessation is driven by weight gain.

section: 6 Interpreting effect sizes: log-odds vs probability scale
text:
6 Interpreting effect sizes: log-odds vs probability scale
The SEM encodes the direct effect of quitting as \(-0.30\) on the log-odds scale. The causal analyses (B and C) report results on the risk difference (probability) scale. These are not directly comparable, and the conversion is non-linear. This section derives the expected probability-scale values from the SEM parameters.

6.1 The delta method approximation
The probability of T2D is linked to the log-odds linear predictor \(\eta\) by the logistic function:
\[P(\text{T2D}) = \sigma(\eta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}}\]
When quit changes from 0 to 1, the linear predictor changes by \(\Delta\eta = -0.30\). The resulting change in probability — the risk difference — is found by differentiating \(\sigma(\eta)\):
\[\frac{d\sigma}{d\eta} = \sigma(\eta)\,(1 - \sigma(\eta)) = P\,(1-P)\]
This is the variance of a Bernoulli random variable at baseline probability \(P\). Applying the delta method:
\[\Delta P \approx P(1-P)\cdot\Delta\eta
           = 0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.30 \approx 0.014\]
The \(P(1-P)\) term controls how sensitive the probability scale is to log-odds changes. It is maximised at \(P=0.5\) (equals \(0.25\)) and shrinks toward zero as the outcome becomes rare or very common:

With a T2D prevalence of ~5% in this cohort, all effects are compressed on the probability scale — a log-odds of \(-0.30\) becomes only \(\approx -0.014\) as a risk difference.


6.2 Approximation error
The delta method linearises the logistic curve. For \(\Delta\eta = -0.30\) the exact calculation is:
\[\eta_0 = \log\!\left(\frac{0.05}{0.95}\right) \approx -2.944\]
\[P(\text{quit}=0) = \sigma(-2.944) = 0.050\]
\[P(\text{quit}=1) = \sigma(-2.944 - 0.30) = \sigma(-3.244) \approx 0.0377\]
\[\Delta P_{\text{exact}} = 0.0377 - 0.050 = -0.0123\]
Versus the delta method approximation of \(-0.014\). The error of \(\approx 0.002\) arises because the logistic curve is concave at \(P=0.05\) — the linear approximation overshoots. The mediation package and g-formula evaluate the logistic function exactly through simulation and prediction, so they will be closer to \(-0.012\) than \(-0.014\).


6.3 What to expect from Analyses B and C
Combining the direct effect (\(-0.30\) log-odds) with the opposing mediated pathway — quitting raises BMI by \(+0.90\) kg/m\(^2\) on average, and each kg/m\(^2\) increases log-odds of T2D by \(+0.20\), contributing \(+0.90 \times 0.20 = +0.18\) log-odds — gives a net log-odds change of \(-0.30 + 0.18 = -0.12\). Converting to the probability scale:
\[\Delta P_{\text{net}} \approx 0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.12 \approx 0.006\]

text:
7 Analysis B — Causal mediation analysis
Using the mediation package (Imai, Keele, and Tingley 2010) to decompose the total effect of quitting into:
\[\text{TE} = \underbrace{\text{ACME}}_{\text{via ΔBMI}} + \underbrace{\text{ADE}}_{\text{direct}}\]


Code
# Mediator model: ΔBMI ~ quit + confounders
med_model <- lm(
  delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort
)

# Outcome model: T2D ~ quit + ΔBMI + confounders
out_model <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)

med_out <- mediate(
  med_model, out_model,
  treat    = "quit",
  mediator = "delta_bmi",
  robustSE = TRUE,
  sims     = 500
)




Code
# Outcome model log-odds coefficients for OR conversion
out_coef <- coef(out_model)

med_tbl <- data.frame(
  Component = c("ACME (BMI-mediated effect)", "ADE (direct effect of quit)",
                "Total effect (ATE)", "Proportion mediated via BMI"),
  `Risk difference` = round(
    c(med_out$d0, med_out$z0, med_out$tau.coef, med_out$n0), 4),
  `95% CI` = c(
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$d0.ci[1],  med_out$d0.ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$z0.ci[1],  med_out$z0.ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", med_out$tau.ci[1], med_out$tau.ci[2]),
    "—"),
  `Note` = c(
    "Harmful offsetting path: BMI gain raises T2D risk",
    sprintf("OR = %.3f from outcome model log-odds = %.3f",
            exp(out_coef["quit"]), out_coef["quit"]),
    "Net effect on probability scale (ADE + ACME)",
    "Fraction of total effect operating via BMI"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

8 Analysis C — G-formula (parametric SCM)
The fully causal approach. For each individual we:

Fit \(E[\Delta\text{BMI} \mid \text{do(quit}=t\text{)}, \mathbf{X}]\) — the mediator model.
Predict \(\widehat{\Delta\text{BMI}}\) under the intervention \(t \in \{0,1\}\).
Plug \(\widehat{\Delta\text{BMI}}\) into the outcome model to predict T2D risk.
Average over the covariate distribution \(\rightarrow\) ATE.

This implements \(E[Y(\text{do}(A=1))]\) rather than \(E[Y \mid A=1]\).


Code
med_gform <- lm(
  delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort
)
out_gform <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)

gformula_ate <- function(df, treat_val) {
  df_int           <- df
  df_int$quit      <- treat_val
  df_int$delta_bmi <- predict(med_gform, newdata = df_int)
  mean(predict(out_gform, newdata = df_int, type = "response"))
}

p_dm_smoke <- gformula_ate(cohort, 0)

  o   <- glm(diabetes  ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
             data = b, family = binomial)
  f   <- function(tv) {
    d <- b; d$quit <- tv; d$delta_bmi <- predict(m, newdata = d)
    mean(predict(o, newdata = d, type = "response"))

  f(1) - f(0)
})

10 Heterogeneous treatment effects (CATE)
Feuerriegel et al. (2024) emphasise conditional ATE (CATE). The claim that high-BMI patients face a larger short-term T2D risk increase from quitting rests on two links in the SEM that must both be visible in the data:

High baseline BMI predicts more post-cessation weight gain — encoded in the mediator equation as 0.15 * (bmi0 - 23) * quit. A patient at BMI = 30 is expected to gain \(0.15 \times 7 = 1.05\) kg/m² extra compared to a patient at BMI = 23.
Greater weight gain increases T2D risk — encoded as +0.20 * bmi_post in the outcome equation.

We verify link (1) directly from the mediator model before computing the full CATE, so the mechanism is transparent rather than implicit.

3 Confounder (Pretreatment covariate)
Treatment selection bias (Confounder) : D->Y, U->D, U->Y. In order to estimate the causal effect of D on Y, we need to close the back door path D<-U->Y. Condition on U to estimate the causal effect. Pearl book, p. 62. Or as in, Angrist and Pischke (p. 57), this is the unconditional average effect obtained by averaging all the X-specific effects weighted by the marginal distribution of X_i.
When trying to find the causal effect of X on Y, we want the nodes we condition on to block any “backdoor” path in which one end has an arrow into X, because such paths may make X and Y dependent, but are obviously not transmitting causal influences from X, and if we do not block them, they will confound the effect that X has on Y.We condition on backdoor paths so as to fulfill our first requirement. However, we don’t want to condition on any nodes that are descendants of X. Descendants of X would be affected by an intervention on X and might themselves affect Y; conditioning
We search for an observed variable that fits the backdoor criterion from D to Y. A brief examination of the graph shows that U, which is not a descendant of D, also blocks the backdoor path D ← U → Y. Therefore, U meets the backdoor criterion. So long as the causal story conforms to the graph. adjusting for U will give us the causal effect of D on Y. Using the adjustment formula, we find
\[ P(Y=y|do(D)) =\sum_U P(Y=y|D=d,U=u) P(U=u) \]
and the average treatment effect (ATE) is
\[ ATE= P(Y=y|do(D=1)) -  P(Y=y|do(D=0)) \]
When confounder is continuous use regression
\[ y = \beta_0+\beta_D D +\beta_U U +\epsilon \] then the estimated \(\beta_D\) is the causal effect of U on Y. Angrist and Pischke (p. 55) : regression can be seen as a matching estimator, capturing an average causal effect, much as the adjustment formula does.

3.7 Partialling out approach
Chern book (see p. 35) analyze wage gap notebook. This can be applied via lasso when U is high dimensional (see DML method for gun ownership in Chern book p.260)
Note that DML requires being able to accurately model the “outcome process,” i.e. the conditional expectation function E[𝑌 | 𝐷, 𝑋]. When the outcome process is hard to model, we might need to use propensity score (see Chern book, 5.3 Identification Using Propensity Scores and Chern book Ch 14.)

Without this condition, there are values 𝑥 in the support of 𝑋 where we cannot construct a contrast between treatment and control units.The conditional probability of receiving treatment, the propensity score, plays an important role in this approach.

title: Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP)
text:
Peters, Bühlmann, and Meinshausen (2016) establish that, under a linear structural equation model (SEM), the set of causal parents of a target variable \(Y\) is the unique subset \(S^*\) of predictors whose regression residuals have the same distribution across all experimental environments:
\[
S^* = \bigcap \bigl\{ S \subseteq \{1,\ldots,p\} :
      H_0(S) \text{ is not rejected} \bigr\}
\]
where \(H_0(S)\) asserts that the residuals of \(Y \sim X_S\) are invariant (same mean, same variance) in every environment \(e \in \mathcal{E}\).
This property holds even in the presence of hidden confounders — the key advantage over standard regression or IRM (Arjovsky et al. (2019)).





Step
Action




1
For every subset \(S \subseteq \{X_1,\ldots,X_p\}\)


2
Fit \(Y \sim X_S\) in each environment; collect residuals


3
Test \(H_0(S)\): residual distribution identical across envs


4
Record all accepted subsets (fail to reject \(H_0\))


5
\(S^* =\) intersection of all accepted subsets

title: Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP)
text:
2 Structural equation model
The synthetic DGP mirrors Figure 1 of Peters, Bühlmann, and Meinshausen (2016):
\[
\begin{aligned}
H   &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)                       &&\text{hidden confounder}\\
X_1 &\leftarrow 0.8\,H + \varepsilon_1            &&\text{causal parent of }Y\\
Y   &\leftarrow 1.5\,X_1 + H + \varepsilon_Y      &&\text{target}\\
X_2 &\leftarrow 0.9\,Y  + \varepsilon_2            &&\text{child of }Y\text{ (non-causal)}\\
X_3 &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)                        &&\text{pure noise}
\end{aligned}
\]
Interventions across environments target \(X_1\) and \(X_3\), never \(Y\) directly. Only \(X_1\) is a true causal parent; \(X_2\) and \(X_3\) are not.

title: Invariant Causal Prediction (ICP)
text:
7 Sensitivity: number of environments
A key theorem in Peters, Bühlmann, and Meinshausen (2016): identifiability of \(S^*\) improves with more environments. With a single environment, no invariance test has power — any subset passes.


Code
run_icp <- function(envs) {
  # Need >=2 environments for any pairwise contrast; 1 env => trivially accept all
  if (length(envs) < 2)
    return("(trivially all accepted — no pairwise contrast with 1 env)")
  res <- lapply(all_subsets, function(S) invariance_test(S, envs)$accepted)
  acc <- all_subsets[unlist(res)]
  if (length(acc) == 0) return("∅ (no subset accepted)")
  s <- Reduce(intersect, acc)
  if (length(s) == 0) "∅" else paste0("{", paste(s, collapse=", "), "}")
}

sens_df <- data.frame(
  Environments = c("E1 only", "E1 + E2", "E1 + E2 + E3"),
  `S* estimate` = c(
    run_icp(env_list["E1"]),
    run_icp(env_list[c("E1","E2")]),
    run_icp(env_list)
  ),
  Interpretation = c(
    "No contrast possible — S* undefined with a single environment",
    "Partially identified",
    "✅ Recovers true causal parent {X1}"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Causal Structures and Matching
text:
2 Simple causal chain
The simplest structure: \(D \rightarrow Y\). No confounding; the regression coefficient for \(D\) directly recovers the causal effect.


Code

  D [pos="0,.1"]
  Y [pos=".2,.1"]
  D -> Y
}')

title: Causal Structures and Matching
text:
3 Confounder (pre-treatment covariate)
Structure: \(D \rightarrow Y\), \(U \rightarrow D\), \(U \rightarrow Y\).
\(U\) is a confounder — it causes both treatment and outcome, opening a back-door path \(D \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y\). Naive comparison of treated and control units conflates the causal effect of \(D\) with the selection effect of \(U\).
Identification strategy: block the back-door path by conditioning on \(U\). The adjustment formula gives:
\[P(Y=y \mid \text{do}(D=d)) = \sum_U P(Y=y \mid D=d, U=u)\,P(U=u)\]
and the ATE is \(E[Y \mid \text{do}(D=1)] - E[Y \mid \text{do}(D=0)]\).
For continuous \(U\), regression adjustment achieves this:
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_D D + \beta_U U + \varepsilon
\quad \Rightarrow \quad \hat\beta_D = \text{causal effect of } D\]


Code
g <- dagitty('dag {
  D [pos="0,.1"]
  Y [pos=".2,.1"]
  U [pos=".1,.2"]
  D -> Y
  D <- U -> Y
}')
plot(g)





Confounder U creates a back-door path from D to Y.





3.1 Simulated data
True SEM:
\[U \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), \quad
  D = \mathbf{1}[U > 0.5], \quad
  Y = 10 + 20\,D + 5\,U + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1.5^2)\]
True causal effect of \(D\): \(\rho = 20\).


Code
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
U <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)

p.overlap <- 0.1
D <- ifelse(U > 0.5,
            ifelse(runif(n) > p.overlap, 1, 0),
            ifelse(runif(n) > p.overlap, 0, 1))

rho <- 20
Y   <- 10 + rho * D + 5 * U + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5)

# Naive (unadjusted) ATE
cat("Non-adjusted ATE (biased):", round(mean(Y[D==1]) - mean(Y[D==0]), 2), "\n")


Non-adjusted ATE (biased): 26.04 


Code
cat("True causal effect (rho):", rho, "\n\n")


True causal effect (rho): 20 


Code
# Covariate balance check
cat("Mean U | D=0:", round(mean(U[D==0]), 3),
    "  Mean U | D=1:", round(mean(U[D==1]), 3), "\n")


Mean U | D=0: -0.369   Mean U | D=1: 0.857 








Why naive comparison is biased here



Because \(D\) is assigned based on \(U\) (high-\(U\) individuals more likely to get \(D=1\)), and \(U\) also directly affects \(Y\), the treated group has higher \(Y\) on average for reasons unrelated to \(D\). The naive difference-in-means overestimates the causal effect.

4 Collider
Structure: \(D \rightarrow U\), \(Y \rightarrow U\).
\(U\) is a collider — both \(D\) and \(Y\) cause it. Conditioning on a collider opens a spurious path between \(D\) and \(Y\) that does not exist in the true DAG. Do not adjust for colliders.

  Y [pos="2,1"]

Collider U: both D and Y cause U. Conditioning on U introduces bias.

5 Post-treatment covariate (mediation)
Structure: \(D \rightarrow U \rightarrow Y\) and \(D \rightarrow Y\).
\(U\) is a mediator — it lies on the causal path from \(D\) to \(Y\). This is the key structure also present in the smoking–BMI–diabetes example: Quit Smoking \(\rightarrow\) \(\Delta\)BMI \(\rightarrow\) T2D.


Code
g_med <- dagitty('dag {
  D [pos="0,1"]
  Y [pos="2,1"]
  U [pos="1,2"]
  D -> Y
  D -> U -> Y
}')
plot(g_med)





Mediation: D affects Y both directly and via mediator U.





5.1 Simulated data
True SEM (linear, continuous outcome):
\[D \sim \text{Bernoulli}(0.5), \quad
  U = 10\,D + \varepsilon_U, \quad
  Y = 10 + 20\,D + 5\,U + \varepsilon_Y\]
The direct effect of \(D\) on \(Y\) is \(\beta_D = 20\). The indirect effect (via \(U\)) is \(\beta_U \times \delta = 5 \times 10 = 50\). The total effect is \(20 + 50 = 70\).


Code
set.seed(7)
n   <- 200
D_m <- ifelse(runif(n) > 0.5, 1, 0)
U_m <- 10 * D_m + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
Y_m <- 10 + 20 * D_m + 5 * U_m + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5)

cat("Mean U | D=1:", round(mean(U_m[D_m==1]), 2),
    "  Mean U | D=0:", round(mean(U_m[D_m==0]), 2), "\n")


Mean U | D=1: 10.11   Mean U | D=0: -0.02 


Code

(U is not balanced — it is caused by D, not a confounder)




5.2 Effect decomposition via regression
Adjusting for mediator \(U\) recovers the direct effect only. Omitting \(U\) recovers the total effect. In the linear case these follow algebraically from the structural coefficients:
\[\text{Direct effect} = \beta_D = 20\] \[\text{Indirect effect} = \beta_U \times \delta = 5 \times 10 = 50\] \[\text{Total effect} = \beta_D + \beta_U \delta = 70\]
where \(\delta = E[U \mid D=1] - E[U \mid D=0]\) is estimated from the auxiliary regression \(U \sim D\).


Code
lm.adj   <- lm(Y_m ~ U_m + D_m)   # direct effect (controls for mediator)
lm.noadj <- lm(Y_m ~ D_m)         # total effect  (omits mediator)

# Auxiliary: how much does D shift U (the mediator)?
delta <- coef(lm(U_m ~ D_m))["D_m"]

  ),

    20, 5 * 10, 70,
    coef(lm.adj)["D_m"],
    coef(lm.adj)["U_m"] * delta,
    coef(lm.noadj)["D_m"]
  ), 2)
), caption = "Regression-based mediation decomposition: direct, indirect, and total effects")

5.3 Causal mediation analysis (mediation package)
The regression approach above works cleanly in the linear case because effects add on the same scale. For non-linear outcomes (e.g. logistic regression in the smoking example) we need the potential-outcomes framework of Imai, Keele, and Tingley (2010). We apply it here to the linear case so the machinery is transparent before the logistic application.
The two estimands are:
\[\text{ACME} = E\bigl[Y_i(1, M_i(1)) - Y_i(1, M_i(0))\bigr]
  \quad \text{(indirect / mediated effect)}\]
\[\text{ADE} = E\bigl[Y_i(1, M_i(0)) - Y_i(0, M_i(0))\bigr]
  \quad \text{(direct effect)}\]
In the linear SEM these reduce to \(\text{ACME} = \beta_U \delta = 50\) and \(\text{ADE} = \beta_D = 20\), matching the regression estimates above.

library(mediation)
df_med <- data.frame(D = D_m, U = U_m, Y = Y_m)

# Step 1: mediator model  M ~ T + C  (no confounders here; D is randomised)
med_lm  <- lm(U ~ D, data = df_med)

# Step 2: outcome model  Y ~ T + M + C
out_lm  <- lm(Y ~ D + U, data = df_med)

# Step 3: mediate() simulates potential outcomes
med_lin <- mediate(med_lm, out_lm,
                   treat    = "D",
                   mediator = "U",
                   sims     = 500)

    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", med_lin$z0.ci[1],  med_lin$z0.ci[2]),
    sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", med_lin$tau.ci[1], med_lin$tau.ci[2]),
    "—"),

5.4 G-formula applied to the linear mediation SEM
In the linear case the g-formula reduces to g-computation: fit models for the mediator and outcome, then predict the outcome under the intervention \(\text{do}(D = t)\) by replacing observed \(U\) with the predicted counterfactual \(\hat U^{(t)}\):
\[\hat U_i^{(t)} = \hat\alpha_0 + \hat\alpha_1\,t\]
\[\hat Y_i^{(t)} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1\,t + \hat\beta_2\,\hat U_i^{(t)}\]
\[\widehat{\text{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \hat Y_i^{(1)}
                         - \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \hat Y_i^{(0)}\]
For a linear SEM this equals the total effect coefficient from the unadjusted regression, but the three-step procedure generalises directly to the logistic case in the smoking example.


Code
# Fit models on observed data
med_gform_lin <- lm(U ~ D,     data = df_med)
out_gform_lin <- lm(Y ~ D + U, data = df_med)

gformula_linear <- function(df, treat_val) {
  d_int   <- df
  d_int$D <- treat_val
  # Step 1: predict mediator under intervention
  d_int$U <- predict(med_gform_lin, newdata = d_int)
  # Step 2: predict outcome using counterfactual mediator
  mean(predict(out_gform_lin, newdata = d_int))
}

y_do1 <- gformula_linear(df_med, 1)
y_do0 <- gformula_linear(df_med, 0)
ate_gf <- y_do1 - y_do0

# Bootstrap CI
set.seed(42)
boot_lin <- replicate(500, {
  b  <- df_med[sample(nrow(df_med), replace = TRUE), ]
  mm <- lm(U ~ D,     data = b)
  om <- lm(Y ~ D + U, data = b)
  f  <- function(tv) {
    d <- b; d$D <- tv; d$U <- predict(mm, newdata = d)
    mean(predict(om, newdata = d))
  }
  f(1) - f(0)
})
ci_lin <- quantile(boot_lin, c(0.025, 0.975))

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Quantity  = c("E[Y | do(D=1)]", "E[Y | do(D=0)]",
                "ATE = do(D=1) − do(D=0)",
                "95% bootstrap CI", "True total effect"),
  Value     = c(round(y_do1, 2), round(y_do0, 2),
                round(ate_gf, 2),
                sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_lin[1], ci_lin[2]),
                "70")
), caption = paste0(

  "The result matches the total effect from unadjusted regression ",
  "and the TE from causal mediation — all three methods agree in the linear case."))

This linear mediation example and the smoking–BMI–diabetes logistic model share the same causal skeleton — \(D \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\) and \(D \rightarrow Y\) — and the same core warning about conditioning on the mediator. The three methods implemented here (regression decomposition, causal mediation package, and g-formula) all agree in the linear case. In the smoking example they are also necessary to align, and the fact that they agree there too confirms the SEM parameters are being recovered correctly.

Key difference 1 — direction of the indirect effect. Here \(D\) increases \(U\) (\(\delta = 10 > 0\)) and \(U\) increases \(Y\) (\(\beta_U = 5 > 0\)), so the indirect path amplifies the total effect: \(\text{TE} = 70 > \text{DE} = 20\). In the smoking example quitting raises \(\Delta\)BMI (\(+0.90\) kg/m²) and raised BMI increases T2D risk (\(+0.20\) log-odds per unit), so the indirect path opposes the direct protective effect of quitting. This produces the clinically important near-zero ATE documented by Hu et al. (2018): the direct benefit of cessation is substantially cancelled in the short term by weight gain.
Key difference 2 — outcome scale. In the linear SEM, ACME and ADE are in units of \(Y\) and add to TE on the same scale. In the logistic SEM, the structural coefficients (\(-0.30\), \(+0.20\)) are on the log-odds scale, but mediation package and g-formula report results on the probability (risk difference) scale. The conversion requires the delta method: \(\Delta P \approx P(1-P) \cdot \Delta\eta \approx 0.05 \times 0.95 \times 0.30 \approx 0.014\), which explains why the ADE of \(\approx -0.012\) looks very different from \(-0.30\).
Key difference 3 — confounding. In this linear example \(D\) is randomised, so no confounder adjustment is needed. In the smoking example, quitting is self-selected (older, more active patients quit more), introducing confounding that must be handled by including \(\mathbf{C}\) in both the mediator and outcome models. The g-formula standardises over the observed confounder distribution to remove this selection bias.
What all three methods tell us in both examples: conditioning on the mediator when estimating the total effect of \(D\) is always wrong — it blocks the \(D \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\) path. The g-formula and mediation package resolve this by explicitly modelling the mediator distribution under intervention and integrating over it, which is exactly what Feuerriegel et al. (2024) call for when embedding ML in a causal framework.

7 Random vs non-random assignment
When treatment is randomly assigned, naive regression recovers the causal effect without adjustment. When assignment depends on a covariate \(x\) (non-random), matching or adjustment is required.


Code
set.seed(10)
n       <- 200
x       <- rnorm(n, 5.5, 0.5)
p.ov    <- 0.1
D.rand  <- ifelse(runif(n) > 0.5, 1, 0)
D.nonr  <- ifelse(x < 5,
                  ifelse(runif(n) > p.ov, 1, 0),
                  ifelse(runif(n) > p.ov, 0, 1))

rho_r <- 5; alpha_r <- 1; gamma_r <- -1
y.rand <- alpha_r + rho_r * D.rand + gamma_r * x + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5)
y.nonr <- alpha_r + rho_r * D.nonr + gamma_r * x + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5)

lm.rand <- lm(y.rand ~ D.rand + x)
lm.nonr <- lm(y.nonr ~ D.nonr + x)

df_r <- data.frame(D = D.nonr, y = y.nonr, x = x)
m_nn  <- matchit(D ~ x, data = df_r, method = "optimal")
m_cem <- matchit(D ~ x, data = df_r, method = "cem")

title: Causal ML for Treatment Outcomes: Smoking, BMI, and Diabetes
text:
Feuerriegel et al. (2024) argue that standard ML pipelines fail when estimating treatment effects because they ignore the causal structure linking treatment, mediators, and outcomes. Their canonical example:

“Consider a patient with a high body mass index whose doctor recommends quitting smoking, and for whom the diabetes risk should be predicted. Literature from traditional ML would suggest using both the body mass index and smoking behavior to predict the diabetes risk under a smoking versus no-smoking scenario; however, this approach would ignore that stopping smoking would also change a patient’s body mass index.”

This document implements a principled causal analysis of exactly that example using three approaches:








Approach
Description
Validity




(A) Naïve ML
Logistic regression on post-treatment BMI
❌ Biased (conditions on mediator)


(B) Causal mediation
Decomposes total effect into direct + BMI-mediated (Imai, Keele, and Tingley 2010)
✅ Correct decomposition


(C) G-formula / SCM
Intervenes do(quit=1), propagates through BMI
✅ Correct counterfactual ATE





The synthetic cohort is calibrated to three published sources:

Hu et al. (2018) (NHS / NHS-II / HPFS cohorts, NEJM): post-cessation weight gain explained ~68% of the transient type 2 diabetes (T2D) spike; HR ≈ 1.91 for quitters with ≥10 kg gain.
Kangbuk Samsung Health Study (2024): mean BMI 25.68 ± 3.53 (T2D) vs 23.18 ± 3.28 (non-T2D); current smokers HR ≈ 1.29.
Bush et al. (2016): post-cessation BMI increase ≈ 0.9 kg/m² within 3 years; magnitude varies with baseline BMI.

3 Causal DAG
The assumed structural equation model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{BMI}_0 &= 23.5 + 0.05(\text{Age}-50) + 1.20\,\text{Sex} + 0.50\,\text{FamHx}
               + 0.04\,\text{Alcohol} - 0.80\,\text{Activity} + \varepsilon_1,
               \quad \varepsilon_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 3.0^2) \\[4pt]
\text{Quit}  &\sim \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(\sigma\!\left(
               -1.2 + 0.015(\text{Age}-50) - 0.20\,\text{Sex}
               + 0.02(\text{BMI}_0 - 23) + 0.30\,\text{Activity}\right)\right) \\[4pt]
\Delta\text{BMI} &= 0.90\,\text{Quit} + 0.05(\text{BMI}_0 - 23)\cdot\text{Quit}
                   + 0.30(1-\text{Activity})\cdot\text{Quit}
                   - 0.15\,\text{Activity} + \varepsilon_2,
                   \quad \varepsilon_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1.2^2) \\[4pt]
\text{logit}\,P(\text{T2D}=1) &= -5.50 + 0.035(\text{Age}-50) + 0.50\,\text{Sex}
               + 0.80\,\text{FamHx} + 0.20\,(\text{BMI}_0 + \Delta\text{BMI} - 23) \\
               &\quad + 0.025\,\text{Alcohol} - 0.40\,\text{Activity}
                 \underbrace{- 0.30\,\text{Quit}}_{\text{direct effect}} + \varepsilon_3,
                 \quad \varepsilon_3 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.3^2)
\end{aligned}
\] The direct causal effect of quitting on T2D is encoded as \(-0.30\) on the log-odds scale. This is not directly comparable to the ATE and ADE reported by the g-formula and causal mediation analysis, which are both on the risk difference (probability) scale. At a baseline T2D prevalence of approximately 5%, a log-odds change of \(-0.30\) translates to a risk difference of roughly \(0.05 \times (1-0.05) \times 0.30 \approx 0.014\). However, the mediated pathway partially offsets this: quitting raises BMI by approximately \(+0.90\) kg/m² on average, and each unit of BMI increases log-odds of T2D by \(+0.20\), contributing an opposing mediated effect of approximately \(0.90 \times 0.20 = +0.18\) log-odds, or \(+0.008\) on the risk difference scale. The expected values on the probability scale are therefore:



Quantity
Expected (probability scale)




ADE — direct protective effect of quitting
≈ −0.010 to −0.015


ACME — harm mediated via BMI gain
≈ +0.005 to +0.010


ATE — net total effect (ADE + ACME)
≈ −0.004 to −0.008



These are exactly the values recovered by the g-formula and causal mediation analysis, confirming that both methods correctly identify the SEM parameters. The near-zero ATE reflects the short-term reality documented by Hu et al. (2018): the direct benefit of cessation is substantially offset by weight gain in the years immediately following quitting.
The key path ignored by naïve ML is Quit → ΔBMI → T2D.


Code
library(ggplot2)

# Node positions
dag_nodes <- data.frame(
  node = c("Quit\nSmoking", "ΔBMI", "Diabetes", "Baseline\nBMI",
           "Age/Sex/\nFam Hx", "Alcohol/\nActivity"),
  x    = c(3, 5, 7, 3, 1, 1),
  y    = c(3, 3, 3, 5, 5, 1)
)

dag_coords <- setNames(dag_nodes[, c("x","y")], c("x","y"))
rownames(dag_coords) <- dag_nodes$node

# Colour palette
pal <- c("mediated" = "#1D9E75",   # green
         "direct"   = "#3B8BD4",   # blue
         "conf"     = "#888780")   # grey

# Helper: nudge start/end away from node centres + optional perpendicular offset
# so parallel edges between the same pair of nodes do not overlap.
nudge <- 0.38
off   <- 0.13   # perpendicular separation

make_edge <- function(fx, fy, tx, ty, type, y_off = 0) {
  dx  <- tx - fx; dy <- ty - fy
  len <- sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2)
  ux  <- dx / len; uy <- dy / len
  # perpendicular unit vector
  px  <- -uy; py <- ux
  data.frame(
    x    = fx + ux * nudge + px * y_off,
    y    = fy + uy * nudge + py * y_off,
    xend = tx - ux * nudge + px * y_off,
    yend = ty - uy * nudge + py * y_off,
    type = type,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

# Confounder edges (grey) — no parallel overlap with coloured edges
conf_pairs <- list(
  c("Baseline\nBMI",     "ΔBMI"),
  c("Baseline\nBMI",     "Diabetes"),
  c("Age/Sex/\nFam Hx",  "Quit\nSmoking"),
  c("Age/Sex/\nFam Hx",  "Diabetes"),
  c("Alcohol/\nActivity", "ΔBMI"),
  c("Alcohol/\nActivity", "Diabetes")
)
edges_conf <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conf_pairs, function(p)
  make_edge(dag_coords[p[1],"x"], dag_coords[p[1],"y"],
            dag_coords[p[2],"x"], dag_coords[p[2],"y"], "conf", 0)
))

# Mediated path: Quit→ΔBMI and ΔBMI→Diabetes — nudged upward (positive offset)
edges_mediated <- rbind(
  make_edge(dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","x"], dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","y"],
            dag_coords["ΔBMI","x"],          dag_coords["ΔBMI","y"],
            "mediated", y_off =  off),
  make_edge(dag_coords["ΔBMI","x"],     dag_coords["ΔBMI","y"],
            dag_coords["Diabetes","x"], dag_coords["Diabetes","y"],
            "mediated", y_off =  off)
)

# Direct effect: Quit→Diabetes as a downward-bowing curve (blue)
# so it is visually separate from the straight green mediated chain
direct_df <- data.frame(
  x    = dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","x"] + nudge,
  y    = dag_coords["Quit\nSmoking","y"],
  xend = dag_coords["Diabetes","x"] - nudge,
  yend = dag_coords["Diabetes","y"]
)

arr <- arrow(length = unit(0.28, "cm"), type = "open", ends = "last")

ggplot() +
  # 1. confounder edges (grey)
  geom_segment(
    data      = edges_conf,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour    = pal["conf"],
    linewidth = 0.7,
    alpha     = 0.75,

    colour    = pal["direct"],

    colour    = pal["mediated"],

4 Synthetic cohort


Code
set.seed(2024)
n <- 2000

# Baseline covariates
age      <- round(rnorm(n, 50, 10))
sex      <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45)          # 1 = male
fam_hx   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.20)         # family history of T2D
alcohol  <- pmax(0, rnorm(n, 8, 5))    # g/day
activity <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.35)         # physically active

# Baseline BMI — smokers slightly leaner (MR evidence, Atkins 2021)
bmi0 <- 23.5 +
  0.05 * (age - 50) + 1.20 * sex + 0.50 * fam_hx +
  0.04 * alcohol   - 0.80 * activity + rnorm(n, sd = 3.0)
bmi0 <- pmax(16, bmi0)

# Treatment: quit smoking
lp_quit <- -1.2 + 0.015*(age-50) - 0.20*sex + 0.02*(bmi0-23) + 0.30*activity
quit    <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_quit))

# Mediator: post-cessation BMI change
# Calibrated to Bush (2016): mean gain ≈ +0.9 kg/m² for quitters
delta_bmi <- 0.90 * quit +
             0.05 * (bmi0 - 23) * quit +   # more gain at higher baseline BMI
             0.30 * (1 - activity) * quit - # sedentary quitters gain more
             0.15 * activity + rnorm(n, sd = 1.2)

bmi_post <- bmi0 + delta_bmi

# Outcome: incident T2D (~5-year risk)
# Calibrated to HR ≈ 1.29 (smokers vs never, Kangbuk Samsung 2024)
# and BMI OR ≈ 1.10 per unit (Hu 2018)
lp_dm <- -5.50 +
  0.035 * (age - 50) + 0.50 * sex + 0.80 * fam_hx +
  0.20  * (bmi_post - 23) + 0.025 * alcohol - 0.40 * activity +
 -0.30  * quit + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)

diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_dm))

cohort <- data.frame(age, sex, fam_hx, alcohol, activity,
                     bmi0, quit, delta_bmi, bmi_post, lp_dm, diabetes)

Why this is wrong

text:
7 Analysis C — G-formula (parametric SCM)
The fully causal approach. For each individual we:

Fit \(E[\Delta\text{BMI} \mid \text{do(quit}=t\text{)}, \mathbf{X}]\) — the mediator model.
Predict \(\widehat{\Delta\text{BMI}}\) under the intervention \(t \in \{0,1\}\).
Plug \(\widehat{\Delta\text{BMI}}\) into the outcome model to predict T2D risk.
Average over the covariate distribution \(\rightarrow\) ATE.

This implements \(E[Y(\text{do}(A=1))]\) rather than \(E[Y \mid A=1]\).


Code
med_gform <- lm(
  delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort
)
out_gform <- glm(
  diabetes ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
  data = cohort, family = binomial
)

gformula_ate <- function(df, treat_val) {
  df_int           <- df
  df_int$quit      <- treat_val
  df_int$delta_bmi <- predict(med_gform, newdata = df_int)
  mean(predict(out_gform, newdata = df_int, type = "response"))
}

p_dm_quit  <- gformula_ate(cohort, 1)
p_dm_smoke <- gformula_ate(cohort, 0)
ate_gform  <- p_dm_quit - p_dm_smoke

# Bootstrap 95% CI
set.seed(42)
boot_ate <- replicate(500, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(cohort), replace = TRUE)
  b   <- cohort[idx, ]
  m   <- lm(delta_bmi ~ quit + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity, data = b)
  o   <- glm(diabetes  ~ quit + delta_bmi + bmi0 + age + sex + fam_hx + alcohol + activity,
             data = b, family = binomial)
  f   <- function(tv) {
    d <- b; d$quit <- tv; d$delta_bmi <- predict(m, newdata = d)
    mean(predict(o, newdata = d, type = "response"))
  }
  f(1) - f(0)
})
ci_gform <- quantile(boot_ate, c(0.025, 0.975))

9 Heterogeneous treatment effects (CATE)
Feuerriegel et al. (2024) emphasise conditional ATE (CATE). Patients with high baseline BMI face greater weight gain after quitting, and thus a larger short-term T2D risk increase — even though quitting is beneficial long-run (Hu et al. 2018).

  p1 <- f(1); p0 <- f(0)
  data.frame(bmi_grp = g, n = nrow(sub),
             p_smoke = p0, p_quit = p1, cate = p1 - p0)

Key takeaway



Naïve ML implicitly assumes BMI is unaffected by the treatment decision. The g-formula correctly propagates do(quit=1) through the mediator ΔBMI, giving a different — and causally valid — population-average risk prediction. The CATE analysis further reveals that the short-term T2D risk from quitting is concentrated in higher-BMI patients, exactly the kind of clinically actionable heterogeneity that causal ML can surface but associational ML misses.

title: Causal ML for Treatment Outcomes: Smoking, BMI, and Diabetes
